explanation_markdown:
## Concept Overview

Lens questions in the Exemplar combine image position, image size, focal length and power. A convex lens can give a real inverted image when the object is outside its focal length and a virtual erect magnified image when the object is inside the focus; a concave lens gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for ordinary real objects. The source also links focal length and power, using shorter positive focal length to represent stronger convergence. Numerical problems become multi-step because magnification first gives one distance relation and the lens formula then determines focal length or the second image position.

## Key Rules & Formulas

- **Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f using the New Cartesian sign convention.** — For a real object, u is negative; for a real image on the opposite side of a convex lens, v is positive; a convex lens has positive f.
- **Lens magnification m = v/u = image height/object height.** — For a real inverted image, magnification is negative; its magnitude gives the size ratio.
- **Power P = 1/f when f is in metres; unit is dioptre.** — Shorter positive focal length means larger positive power and stronger convergence.
- **A convex lens gives a magnified virtual image when the object lies between optical centre and focus, and can give a magnified real image when the object lies between f and 2f.** — The source explicitly asks students to distinguish these two placements.

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** A candle flame forms an image on a screen on the other side of a lens. The image is three times the size of the flame and is 80 cm from the lens. At what distance should the candle be placed? What is the nature of the image and lens?

*Solution:* Because the image is on a screen, it is real and inverted, so m=-3. For a lens, m=v/u; with v=+80 cm, -3=80/u, giving u=-80/3≈-26.7 cm. Then 1/f=1/v-1/u=1/80+3/80=4/80=1/20, so f=+20 cm. Positive focal length identifies a convex lens; the image is real, inverted and magnified.

**Example 2:** A student records: candle position 12.0 cm, convex lens 50.0 cm, screen 88.0 cm. (i) Find focal length. (ii) If candle is shifted to 31.0 cm, where is the image formed? (iii) What happens if it is shifted still closer to the lens?

*Solution:* Initially u=12-50=-38 cm and v=88-50=+38 cm. Thus 1/f=1/38-(-1/38)=2/38=1/19, so f=19 cm. At candle position 31 cm, u=31-50=-19 cm, exactly equal to -f; emergent rays are parallel and the image is at infinity. If the candle is moved still closer so that its distance is less than f, the convex lens forms a virtual, erect and magnified image on the same side as the object.

**Example 3:** Two lenses have focal lengths 20 cm and 40 cm. Which should be used to obtain more convergent light?

*Solution:* For converging lenses, power increases as focal length decreases because P=1/f in metres. A focal length of 20 cm is 0.20 m, giving 5 D, while 40 cm is 0.40 m, giving 2.5 D. Therefore the 20 cm lens has greater converging power.

## What Makes Exemplar Questions on This Topic Harder

Exemplar lens questions often make students infer the device or image type from qualitative clues before calculating anything. Numerical questions combine magnification with the lens formula or use measured laboratory positions, while conceptual questions ask how the screen must move when the object changes. The difficulty lies in sign discipline and in linking algebra to the physical image—real versus virtual, erect versus inverted, and converging strength.

## Common Mistakes

- **Using all distances as positive.** — Students use lengths without applying the sign convention. *How to avoid:* Assign u, v and f signs before substituting; for a real object u is negative.
- **Ignoring the sign of magnification when an image is formed on a screen.** — Only the size ratio is noticed. *How to avoid:* A screen image is real and inverted, so magnification is negative.
- **Thinking a larger focal length means stronger convergence.** — “Larger” is incorrectly associated with “stronger”. *How to avoid:* Use P=1/f: shorter positive focal length gives greater positive power.
- **Trying to form a screen image when the object is inside the focal length of a convex lens.** — Students forget that this case produces a virtual image. *How to avoid:* If |u|<f for a convex lens, expect a virtual, erect, magnified image on the object side.

## Problem-Solving Strategy

Decide first whether the stated image is real or virtual and assign signs accordingly. Use magnification to relate u and v when image size is given, then use the lens formula for focal length or image position. If the object crosses the focus, pause and change the expected image type before doing arithmetic. For power questions, convert centimetres to metres before using P=1/f.

## Quick Recall

Screen image → real and inverted. Convex lens: object inside f gives virtual magnified image; at f gives image at infinity. Power is reciprocal focal length in metres, so shorter f means stronger convergence.

## Practice Problem

**Problem:** A convex lens of focal length 20 cm can produce a magnified virtual as well as a magnified real image. Where should the object be placed in each case?

**Hint:** The two magnified cases lie on opposite sides of the focal point in terms of object distance.

**Answer:** For a magnified virtual image, place the object between the optical centre and focus. For a magnified real image, place it between the focus and twice the focal length.
